entry: English novelist and poet. Trained as an architect, he gained fame with novels in the tradition of [[George Eliot]] that depict rural life and tragic characters struggling against their passions and social circumstances. Many are set in the semi-fictional region of [[Wessex]], initially based on the medieval Anglo-Saxon kingdom and later covering much of southwest and south central England. His major novels include *Far from the Madding Crowd* (1874), *The Return of the Native* (1878), *The Mayor of Casterbridge* (1886), *Tess of the d'Urbervilles* (1891) and *Jude the Obscure* (1895). His first poetry collection appeared in 1898, and younger poets regarded him as a mentor. After his death, his poems were praised by [[Ezra Pound]], W. H. Auden and Philip Larkin. *Tess of the d'Urbervilles* and *Far from the Madding Crowd* were both listed in the top 50 of the BBC's *The Big Read* survey of best-loved novels.

English biologist and anthropologist. Known as "Darwin's Bulldog" for his advocacy of [[Charles Darwin]]'s theory of [[Evolution]], Huxley was a leading comparative anatomist who worked on invertebrates and vertebrates, including the relationship between apes and humans. After comparing [[Archaeopteryx]] with *Compsognathus*, he concluded that birds evolved from small carnivorous dinosaurs. He was largely self-taught. Accounts of his 1860 Oxford debate with Samuel Wilberforce became a key moment in the wider acceptance of evolution, though some historians think aspects of the surviving story are a later fabrication. Huxley coined the term [[Agnosticism|agnosticism]] in 1869 and elaborated on it in 1889. He also helped develop scientific education in Britain and belonged to the prominent Huxley family of scientists and writers.

English philosopher and political theorist. Best known for *Leviathan* (1651), in which he formulated an influential version of social contract theory, Hobbes is considered one of the founders of modern [[Political philosophy|political philosophy]]. He described the state of nature as a "war of all against all" and argued that the solution to human conflict was governance by an absolute sovereign. His views were shaped by the [[English Civil War]] (1642–1651), which he witnessed after returning to England from France in 1637. His other works include the trilogy *De Cive* (1642), *De Corpore* (1655) and *De Homine* (1658). He contributed to history, [[Geometry|geometry]], optics, theology, ethics and classical translation, and is regarded as a polymath. Accusations of atheism and contentious debates with contemporaries marked his career.

Founding Father and third president of the United States, 1801–1809. Principal author of the Declaration of Independence (1776), Jefferson was a prolific writer and philosopher whose political thought formed the basis of Jeffersonian democracy. He served as the first U.S. Secretary of State under [[George Washington]] and as vice president under [[John Adams]]. With [[James Madison]], he founded the [[Democratic-Republican Party]] in 1792. As president he promoted western expansion through the [[Louisiana Purchase]], which doubled the nation's size, and supported the [[Lewis and Clark Expedition]]. He also implemented the Embargo Act of 1807 to protect American shipping and industry. Jefferson owned large numbers of slaves throughout his life, and historians offer varying interpretations of his views on slavery. Scholars and public opinion rank him among the upper tier of U.S. presidents.

German preacher and theologian of the early Reformation. He opposed both [[Martin Luther]] and the [[Catholic Church]], and by 1523 had completely broken with Luther over Luther's compromises with feudal authority. Müntzer believed that the end of the world was imminent and that true believers must aid God in ushering in a new era of history. In 1525 he organized an armed militia at Mühlhausen and became a leader of the German peasant and plebeian uprising known as the German Peasants' War. He was captured after the Battle of Frankenhausen, tortured and executed. Few figures of the German Reformation have raised as much controversy, and he is now regarded as a significant personality in the early years of the Reformation and in the history of European revolutionaries.

German novelist and Nobel laureate. Awarded the 1929 Nobel Prize in Literature, Mann wrote symbolic and ironic epic novels and novellas that probe the psychology of the artist and the intellectual. His first novel, *Buddenbrooks* (1901), portrays his own Hanseatic family and its merchant class. Later works include *Death in Venice* (1912), *The Magic Mountain* (1924), the tetralogy *Joseph and His Brothers* (1933–1943) and *Doctor Faustus* (1947). His analysis of the German and European soul drew on the ideas of [[Johann Wolfgang von Goethe]], [[Friedrich Nietzsche]] and [[Arthur Schopenhauer]]. After [[Adolf Hitler]] came to power in 1933, Mann fled to Switzerland. He moved to the United States in 1939 and returned to Switzerland in 1952. He is one of the best-known exponents of *Exilliteratur*, German literature written in exile by those who opposed the Hitler regime.

English lawyer, statesman and Renaissance humanist. He served as Lord Chancellor to [[Henry VIII]] from 1529 to 1532. His book *Utopia* (1516) describes the political system of an imaginary island state. More opposed the Protestant Reformation, directing polemics against [[Martin Luther]], Huldrych Zwingli and William Tyndale, and he opposed Henry VIII's separation from the [[Catholic Church]]. He refused to take the Oath of Supremacy, which affirmed the king as supreme head of the [[Church of England]]. After being convicted of treason on evidence he said was false, he was executed. Pope Pius XI canonized him as a martyr in 1935, and [[Pope John Paul II]] declared him patron saint of statesmen and politicians in 2000.

English-born American political philosopher and Founding Father. Paine emigrated to the American colonies in 1774 with the help of [[Benjamin Franklin]]. His pamphlet *Common Sense* (1776) argued for independence from Great Britain, and his series *The American Crisis* (1776–1783) supported the patriot cause during the [[American Revolution]]. In *Rights of Man* (1791) he defended the French Revolution against [[Edmund Burke]], and he was convicted in absentia of seditious libel in England in 1792. Elected to the French National Convention, he was arrested in 1793 and released in 1794 through the diplomacy of [[James Monroe]]. In *The Age of Reason* he advocated [[Deism]] and criticized Christian doctrine, alienating many former allies. He returned to the United States in 1802 and was broadly ostracized; only six mourners attended his funeral.

English economist and Anglican cleric. In *An Essay on the Principle of Population* (1798), Malthus argued that gains in food production were temporary because they led to population growth, which restored the earlier level of production per person. Populations tended to grow until the poor suffered hardship, [[Famine]], disease and war, a pattern later called the "Malthusian trap." He criticized the Poor Laws for causing inflation rather than improving the well-being of the poor, and he supported taxes on grain imports, the Corn Laws. Pioneers of evolutionary biology, including [[Charles Darwin]] and [[Alfred Russel Wallace]], read him. His failure to predict the [[Industrial Revolution]] was a frequent criticism, yet his work is described as the theoretical foundation of conventional thinking on global hunger and famine for almost two centuries.

Burkinabé military officer and Marxist revolutionary, president of Burkina Faso, 1983–1987. After a 1983 coup, Sankara launched social, ecological and economic reforms that he called the people's democratic revolution. In 1984 he renamed the country Burkina Faso, meaning "land of the upright people." His foreign policy stressed anti-imperialism and self-reliance, and he rejected loans from the [[International Monetary Fund]]. Domestic programs included famine prevention, land reform, suspension of rural poll taxes, a literacy campaign and vaccinations against meningitis, yellow fever and measles. His government also banned female circumcision, forced marriages and polygamy, and it planted more than 10 million trees to combat desertification of the [[Sahel]]. Amnesty International criticized alleged human rights violations, including arbitrary detentions. Sankara was assassinated in 1987 by troops led by Blaise Compaoré, who held power until the 2014 uprising. In 2021 a military tribunal found Compaoré guilty of Sankara's murder.

English statesman and Catholic cardinal. Royal almoner after [[Henry VIII]] became king in 1509, Wolsey controlled most matters of state by 1514. He was made a cardinal in 1515 and served as Lord Chancellor, the king's chief adviser, in which role he was often depicted as the *alter rex* ("other king"). After failing to negotiate an annulment of Henry's marriage to [[Catherine of Aragon]], he lost favour and was stripped of his government titles. He died from natural causes while on the way to London to answer charges of treason.

British polymath. Young made notable contributions to vision, light, solid mechanics, energy, physiology, language, musical harmony and Egyptology. He is credited with establishing [[Christiaan Huygens]]' wave theory of light, in contrast to the corpuscular theory of [[Isaac Newton]]. In 1801 he proposed a trichromatic theory of color vision and identified astigmatism, and in 1807 he formulated [[Young's modulus]], a measure of a material's stiffness. In 1814 he deciphered the demotic script of the [[Rosetta Stone]] and identified phonetic values in hieroglyphs. His work influenced [[Hermann von Helmholtz]], [[James Clerk Maxwell]] and [[Albert Einstein]]. Young also practiced as a physician and was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society in 1794.

Philosophical and theological school arising from the work of [[Thomas Aquinas]]. Thomism holds that truths accessible through natural reason, such as God's existence and the immortality of the soul, complement divine revelation. Aquinas's commentaries on [[Aristotle]] and his *Summa Theologica* are among his best-known works, and the latter remains a central reference for Catholic philosophy and theology. Its ethics advances natural law theory, and its metaphysics stresses the real distinction between essence and existence. In his 1914 motu proprio *Doctoris Angelici*, Pope Pius X cautioned that the teachings of the Church cannot be understood without the basic philosophical principles of Thomas's major theses. Pope Leo XIII's *Aeterni Patris* (1879) proclaimed Aquinas the "chief and master" of Scholastic philosophy and promoted its revival, and neo-Thomism shaped 20th-century Catholic thought.

Germanic god associated with thunder. In Norse mythology, Thor is a hammer-wielding god associated with thunder, storms, strength, protection, fertility and farmers. His name appears in Old English as Thunor and in Old High German as Donar, from a Proto-Germanic word meaning "thunder." During the [[Viking Age]], amulets of his hammer, Mjölnir, were worn, and many personal names contained his name. Medieval Icelandic sources describe him as the son of [[Odin]] and the husband of the goddess Sif. His exploits include battles with giants and with the Midgard Serpent, Jörmungandr, and the two are prophesied to kill each other at Ragnarök. The day of the week [[Thursday]] derives its name from him, and he is revived in modern [[Heathenry (new religious movement)|Heathenry]].

Body region between the neck and abdomen in mammals and other tetrapods. The thorax, also called the chest, contains the heart, lungs, thymus gland and other organs. The human thoracic cavity is enclosed by the thoracic wall, a framework formed by 12 thoracic vertebrae, the sternum and 12 pairs of ribs that expands and contracts during breathing. In [[Insect|insects]], [[Crustacean|crustaceans]] and the extinct [[Trilobite|trilobites]], the thorax is one of three main body divisions, each made of several segments. The term derives from the Ancient Greek word for "breastplate." The chest may be affected by many diseases, and the most common symptom of these is chest pain.

Weakly radioactive metallic element, atomic number 90 (symbol Th). A light silver metal that tarnishes olive grey in air, thorium is moderately soft and has a high melting point. All its isotopes are unstable; the most stable, thorium-232, has a half-life of 14.0 billion years. [[Jöns Jacob Berzelius]] discovered it in 1828 in a mineral from Norway and named it after the Norse god [[Thor]]. It is estimated to be over three times as abundant as uranium in the Earth's crust. Its radioactivity led to its replacement in many uses in the second half of the 20th century. It is still used as an alloying element in TIG welding electrodes and in strengthening magnesium, and it has been proposed as a replacement for uranium as nuclear fuel, with several thorium reactors built.

Horse breed developed for racing. The word is sometimes used for any purebred horse, but technically refers only to this breed. Developed in 17th- and 18th-century England, it arose from native mares crossed with imported Arabian, Barb and Turkoman stallions. All modern Thoroughbreds trace their pedigrees to three imported stallions. The breed spread worldwide in the 18th and 19th centuries and reached North America in 1730. Thoroughbreds are used mainly for [[Horse racing|racing]] but also for show jumping, dressage, [[Polo]] and fox hunting, and they have influenced many other breeds through [[Selective breeding|crossbreeding]]. Racing at maximum exertion has led to high accident rates and health problems such as bleeding from the lungs, and the breed also has low fertility.

Ancient Egyptian deity of the Moon, wisdom and writing. Thoth was often depicted as a man with the head of an [[Ibis]] or a [[Baboon]], animals sacred to him. He was the god of the Moon, wisdom, knowledge, writing, hieroglyphs, science, magic, art and judgement. His chief temple was at Hermopolis. In Egyptian mythology he maintained the universe and was one of the two deities, the other being Ma'at, who stood on either side of [[Ra]]'s solar barque. In later periods he became associated with arbitrating divine disputes and with the judgment of the dead. In the Greco-Roman period he was syncretized with the Greek god [[Hermes]] as Hermes Trismegistus.

Imaginary scenario meant to elucidate or test an argument or theory. A thought experiment is often an experiment that would be hard, impossible or unethical to perform, and it can also be an abstract hypothetical that tests intuitions about morality or other philosophical questions. The term *Gedankenexperiment* was introduced by physicist [[Ernst Mach]] in 1897. Einstein's elevator scenario illustrated equivalence in [[General relativity|general relativity]], and [[Schrödinger's cat]] highlights interpretive challenges in [[Quantum mechanics]]. Galileo's visualization of bodies falling from the Leaning Tower of Pisa refuted Aristotelian physics. Proponents argue that such scenarios enable rigorous deduction from causal premises, while critics contend that their evidential value depends on untested assumptions about mental simulation.

Long, fine strand of fibers used for joining, creating or decorating textiles. Ancient Egyptians made thread from plant fibers, wool and hair. Modern thread is made from materials including [[Cotton]], [[Wool]], flax, [[Nylon]], [[Silk]] and [[Polyester]], and metal threads can be made of fine wire. Thread is generally fine and smooth enough for [[Sewing]], [[Embroidery]], weaving or making lace, while [[Yarn]] is thicker and softer and suited to knitting and crochet. Thread weight is measured as the length in kilometers that weighs one kilogram, so a higher number means a finer thread. Denier counts the grams in 9,000 meters, and a higher number means a thicker thread.

Hydroelectric gravity dam spanning the Yangtze River in Hubei province, China. Completed in 2006, the dam is 185 meters high and 2,309 meters wide. Its power plant became fully operational in 2012, and its 32 main turbines give it an installed capacity of 22,500 MW, the largest of any [[Power station]] in the world. It generates an average of 95±20 TWh of [[Electricity]] per year, depending on precipitation in the basin. The dam improves shipping on the [[Yangtze]] and provides flood control for millions of people. Estimates of the number of people displaced by its construction range from 1.13 million to around 1.4 million, and construction inundated culturally significant sites. Its ecological effects include an increased risk of landslides.

Period of Chinese history from 220 to 280. After the collapse of the [[Han dynasty]], China was divided among Cao Wei, Shu Han and Eastern Wu. The period was marked by relative stability until Wei conquered Shu in 263, Jin usurped Wei in 266, and Jin conquered Wu in 280. A census taken in 280 counted 2,459,840 households and 16,163,863 individuals, far fewer than the 10,677,960 households and 56,486,856 individuals recorded in the Han era. Technology advanced, and [[Zhuge Liang]] is credited with the wooden ox, suggested to be an early wheelbarrow. The main historical record is Chen Shou's *Records of the Three Kingdoms* (c. 290), annotated in 429 by Pei Songzhi. The best-known fictional account is *Romance of the Three Kingdoms*, a historical novel written in the [[Ming dynasty]] by Luo Guanzhong.

Pre-unification kingdoms of the Korean Peninsula, 57 BC–AD 668. Goguryeo, Paekche and Silla, known as the Samhan, competed for hegemony over the peninsula and roughly half of Manchuria. Goguryeo controlled the northern half of the peninsula, while Paekche and Silla occupied the south. The kingdoms shared a similar culture and language, and all had a warrior aristocracy. [[Buddhism]] became the state religion of all three, starting with Goguryeo in 372. Silla allied with the [[Tang dynasty|Tang]] and unified the peninsula in the 7th century. Silla was later divided into the Later Three Kingdoms and was ultimately annexed by the new Goguryeo revivalist state of [[Goryeo]].

Mythological divine rulers of ancient China. According to Chinese mythology and traditional historiography, the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors were a series of sage rulers and the first emperors of China. They are now considered culture heroes, but in ancient times they were widely worshipped as divine ancestral spirits. The Three Sovereigns were demigods who helped create humankind and imparted essential skills and knowledge. The Five Emperors were exemplary sages of a golden age when the human and divine orders communicated. Their period preceded the [[Xia dynasty]], when the abdication system was used before Qi of Xia seized power and established a hereditary monarchy. Figures from the period were later thought to aid the Chinese people in the [[Shang dynasty]] and the [[Zhou dynasty]].

Problem in classical mechanics of predicting the motion of three gravitating bodies. Given the initial positions and velocities of three point masses, the problem is to calculate their subsequent trajectories using [[Newton's laws of motion]] and [[Newton's law of universal gravitation]]. Unlike the two-body problem, it has no general closed-form analytic solution. For most initial conditions the system is [[Chaos theory|chaotic]], and its motions can only be estimated by [[Numerical integration]]. It is a special case of the n-body problem. The first such problem studied extensively involved the Earth, the Moon and the Sun.
